chunks: And it was also narrated from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

He was asked about a man whose time for prayer entered while he was traveling, so he delayed the prayer until he arrived home, intending to pray it when he reached his family. However, he forgot to pray it upon arrival until the time had passed. He said: 'He should pray it two rak'at as the prayer of a traveler, because the time entered while he was a traveler, and it was incumbent upon him to pray at that time.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a traveler who forgets to pray until the time passes after arriving home?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Baqir (AS), transmitted via the reliable chain of Zurara, clarifies that the ruling for a delayed prayer depends on the traveler's status at the time the prayer's entry occurred, not at the time of performance. Consequently, the make-up prayer retains the two-rak'at format of travel (Qasr) because the obligation arose while the individual was still in the state of journeying. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that the legal status of the prayer is fixed at its onset, ensuring consistency in ritual practice for travelers.
